summary: This work presents a comprehensive design framework for scalable fluxonium quantum processors using double-transmon couplers (DTCs), addressing the scalability challenges that arise from competing demands of strong coupling, qubit isolation, and wiring density. The framework employs frequency-partitioned architecture and multi-objective optimization to simultaneously achieve single-qubit fidelities $F_{1q} > 99.99\%$, two-qubit MAP-gate fidelities $F_{2q} > 99.9\%$, leakage $\eta < 10^{-3}$, fast reset ($t_{\mathrm{reset}} < 300$ ns), and spectator crosstalk suppression ($\zeta < 10$ kHz.
motivation: Fluxonium qubits offer long coherence times and strong anharmonicity, but scaling them to 2D arrays requires simultaneously satisfying competing constraints: strong tunable coupling via DTCs for fast gates, qubit isolation to suppress crosstalk, and adequate spacing for control wiring—a problem not rigorously addressed at the system level.
method: A frequency-allocation scheme separates qubit transitions ($\omega_{0,1}^j < 3$ GHz), plasmon modes ($\omega_{1,2}^j \approx 4.2$ GHz), DTC operational modes ($\omega_{\mathrm{on/off}}^c$), reset resonators ($\omega_r' \approx 3.45$ GHz), and readout resonators ($\omega_r \approx 7.5$ GHz) into distinct spectral bands, enabling a tractable sequential optimization workflow that maps 16 circuit parameters (fluxonium $E_C, E_J, E_L$; DTC parameters; coupling strengths $J_{j,c}/h = 500$ MHz; resonator properties) to experimentally relevant performance metrics while accounting for fabrication disorder.
result: Optimal parameters satisfy all DiVincenzo criteria: $E_J^j/h = 4.65$ GHz, $E_L^j/h = 0.65$ GHz, $E_C^j/h = 1.1$ GHz for fluxoniums; $\omega_{\mathrm{on}}^c = \omega_{1,2}^j \approx 4.23$ GHz (on-resonance) with large detuning $(\omega_{\mathrm{off}}^c - \omega_{1,2}^j)/2\pi \approx 1.8$ GHz to suppress spectator crosstalk; readout dispersive shift $|2\chi|/2\pi \approx 2.55$ MHz with critical photon number $n_{\mathrm{crit}} \approx 75$; reset fidelity $F_{\mathrm{reset}} > 99\%$ in $\approx 300$ ns using $g_r'/2\pi = 50$ MHz, $Q' = 400$.
